title: Functions & modules
summary: Write reusable, named blocks of code — pass them inputs, get results back, and organise your work into modules.
objectives: Define and call your own functions with the def keyword
Pass information in with parameters and arguments
Return results and understand the difference between print and return
Use default and keyword arguments to make functions flexible
Reuse code across files with modules and import

quiz.q: What keyword defines a function in Python?
quiz.why: def (short for define) starts a function definition, followed by the name, parentheses, and a colon.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a parameter and an argument?
quiz.answer: A parameter is the name in the function definition; an argument is the actual value you pass when calling.
quiz.why: def greet(name) — name is a parameter; greet("Dami") — "Dami" is the argument.

quiz.q: What does a function return if it has no return statement?
quiz.why: A function with no explicit return automatically returns the special value None.

quiz.q: True or false — a variable created inside a function can be used after the function finishes.
quiz.why: False. Such variables are local and disappear once the function returns.

resources.label: Python Crash Course (Eric Matthes) — Chapter 8: Functions
Real Python — Defining Your Own Python Function

body_markdown:
## Why functions?

A **function** is a reusable, named block of code. You write a piece of logic once, give it a name, and run it whenever you need it. Without functions you would copy and paste the same lines everywhere — and a bug means fixing every copy.

As a maths graduate this feels natural: a function takes an **input**, does something, and produces an **output** — like *f(x) = x²*.

## Defining and calling a function

Use `def`, a name, parentheses, and a colon. The indented block is the **body**. Defining does not run it — you **call** it with its name and parentheses.

```python
def greet():
    print("Hello, world!")

greet()   # call it
```

## Parameters and arguments

The names inside the parentheses are **parameters**; the values you pass are **arguments**.

```python
def greet(name):
    print("Hello, " + name + "!")

greet("Dami")
```

## Returning values

`return` hands a value back. Note: `print` only shows text; `return` gives back a value you can store.

```python
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

total = add(3, 4)   # 7
```

## Scope and modules

Variables made inside a function are **local** and vanish when it ends. A **module** is a Python file of functions you `import` elsewhere — and the standard library gives you thousands for free.

```python
import math
print(math.sqrt(16))   # 4.0
```

## Your task

Take one of your earlier scripts and **rewrite it using functions**.

slides.title: Functions in Python
slides.narration: Welcome to Month One of your journey from maths graduate to A I engineer. In this lesson we'll cover one of the most important ideas in all of programming: functions. By the end you'll know how to write your own functions, pass them information, get results back, and organise your code into reusable modules.

slides.title: Why functions?
bullets: A function is a reusable, named block of code.
Write the logic once, call it many times.
Shorter, clearer, easier to fix.
Like maths: input goes in, output comes out.
slides.narration: So why do we need functions? Imagine a piece of logic you use again and again. Without functions you'd copy and paste it everywhere, and fixing a bug would mean changing every copy. A function lets you write that logic once, name it, and reuse it. As a maths graduate this will feel familiar: input goes in, output comes out.

slides.title: Defining a function
bullets: Use def, a name, parentheses, and a colon.
The indented block is the body.
Calling it runs that body.
slides.narration: Here's how we define a function. We use the keyword def, followed by a name we choose, then parentheses, then a colon. Everything indented underneath is the body. Defining a function does not run it. To run it, we call it by writing its name followed by parentheses.

slides.title: Parameters and arguments
bullets: Parameters are the inputs in the parentheses.
Arguments are the values you pass in.
This makes a function flexible.
slides.code:
def greet(name):
    print("Hello, " + name + "!")

greet("Dami")
greet("Ada")
slides.narration: Functions become powerful when they take inputs. The names inside the parentheses are called parameters. When we call the function, the real values we hand over, like Dami or Ada, are called arguments. The same function now greets anyone.

slides.title: Returning values
bullets: Use return to send a result back.
Store the returned value in a variable.
No return means the function gives back None.
slides.code:
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

total = add(3, 4)
print(total)   # 7
slides.narration: Often we want a function to give a value back, not just do something. That's what return does. Here, add takes two numbers and returns their sum. We capture the result in a variable and print seven. If a function has no return, it gives back the special value None.

slides.title: Default & keyword arguments
bullets: Defaults are used when no argument is given.
Keyword arguments name the value explicitly.
Both make functions easier to call.
slides.code:
def greet(name, greeting="Hello"):
    return greeting + ", " + name

greet("Dami")
greet("Dami", greeting="Hi")
slides.narration: You can give parameters default values. Here greeting defaults to Hello. If we don't supply one, Python uses that default. We can also pass arguments by name, which we call keyword arguments. Writing greeting equals Hi makes our intent crystal clear.

slides.title: Scope: local vs global
bullets: Variables inside a function are local to it.
They disappear once the function finishes.
Pass data in, return data out.
slides.code:
def square(x):
    result = x * x
    return result

print(square(5))   # 25
slides.narration: Here's a concept that trips up beginners: scope. A variable you create inside a function only exists inside that function. We call it local. Once the function finishes, it's gone. The clean habit is to pass data in through parameters and send data out through return.

slides.title: Modules: reuse across files
bullets: A module is a Python file with functions.
Import it to reuse those functions.
The standard library gives thousands for free.
slides.code:
import mymath
print(mymath.add(2, 3))   # 5

import math
print(math.sqrt(16))      # 4.0
slides.narration: Once you have useful functions, you'll want them across different files. That's what modules are for. A module is simply a Python file containing functions. You bring it in using import. Python's standard library gives you thousands of ready-made functions for free, just an import away.

slides.title: Common mistakes
bullets: Defining a function but never calling it.
Confusing print and return.
Forgetting the colon or wrong indentation.
Expecting a local variable to exist outside.
slides.narration: Let's flag the mistakes that catch nearly everyone. One: defining a function but never calling it. Two: confusing print and return. Print shows text; return hands a value back. Three: forgetting the colon or getting indentation wrong. And four: expecting a local variable to exist outside its function. Watch for these and you'll save hours.

slides.title: Recap & your task
bullets: def names a reusable block; call it with ().
Parameters take input; return sends output.
Defaults and keywords make calls flexible.
Modules let you reuse and import functions.
Task: rewrite a past script using functions.
slides.narration: Let's recap. The def keyword defines a reusable block you run by calling it. Parameters let you pass information in, and return sends a result back. Defaults and keyword arguments make your functions flexible. And modules let you reuse functions across your whole project. Your task before the next lesson: take an earlier script and rewrite it using functions. Great work, and I'll see you in the next lesson.
